History · Issue 14

The Salt Roads of the Outer Sound

Before the railway, every barrel of herring left the islands by sail. The old routes are still on the chart.

MO
Maren Okafor10 November 2026 · 8 min read

For three hundred years, everything that left the outer islands left by sail. Herring went out in barrels, salt came in by the sack, and the routes between them were so well worn that pilots spoke of them as roads: the Long Road around the north of Skerry Holm, the Short Road through the narrows, the Widow’s Road that you took only when the others were closed.

The roads are still on the chart if you know where to look. Old leading marks — a white-painted rock, a cairn on a ridge, a gable end lined up with a church tower — still mark the safe water, though most of the buildings they once pointed at are ruins.

We spent a week following the Short Road with a facsimile of an 1880s pilot book and a handheld compass. Some of the marks have gone. Most have not. And on the last afternoon, lined up exactly as the book described, the church tower at Saltness appeared over the shoulder of the headland, as it has for every sailor who came this way before us. ■
